# Assignment 3

## Part 1 - Plot of real data
The following plot is showing plasma glucose concentration on age where observations are colored by diabetes levels.
```{r Part1, fig.width=12}
```

### Do you think that diabetes is easy to classify by a standard logistic regression model that uses these two variables as features?

There is a lot of overlap in the points on the plot which makes a standard logistic regression hard. There are cases of diabetes spread very evenly across all data points and there is no clear linear relationship between them.

## Part 2 - Logistic regression prediction
In part 2 of assignment 3 we train a logistic regression model. The following plot has the same data points as the previous but are colored according to the predicted diabetes levels from the model:
```{r Part2, fig.width=12}
```

### Report the probabilistic equation of the estimated model (i.e., how the target depends on the features and the estimated model parameters probabilistically).

The probabilistic equation for the estimation of diabetes in the model can be calculated as:
$$
P(y=1 \mid x) 
= \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2)}}
$$
where β0 = (Intercept), β1 = first parameter, β2 = second parameter, with the following values:


```{r}
coef(model1)
```

With the prediction threshold r=0.5 all predictions above 0.5 are classified as "diabetes" while the prediction below it are classified as "not diabetes".

### Misclassification of the model
The training misclassification rate is calculated with given code from lecture slides 1.c.
```{r misclassification}
```

### Comments on the quality of the model
From the predictions it looks like once you go over 120-150 plasma glucose concentration (depending on age) you are predicted to have diabetes. Diabetes is a life-altering disease which you do not want to predict wrong. The misclassification is calculated at about 26.5%. An incorrect prediction 1 in 4 times is not very good in this situation.

## Part 3 - Decision boundary
The equation for the decision boundary can be derived by solving the probabilistic equation of the estimated model in regards to x2: 
$$
x_2 = \frac{\log\!\left(\frac{r}{1 - r}\right) - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_1}{\beta_2}
$$
Adding the decision boundary to the plot gives a perfectly split between the two classifications.
```{r Part3, fig.width=12}
```

## Part 4 - Adjustment of prediction threshold
```{r Part4, fig.width=12}
```

By adjusting the prediction threshold we change how confident the model needs to be to predict a point as "diabetes".

With r=0.2 the model will predict all points that have above 20% risk of diabetes as "diabetes".
With r=0.8 the model will predict all points that have above 80% risk of diabetes as "diabetes".


## Part 5 - Basis function expansion
In the scatterplot for the prediction from the model with expanded features the decision boundary has turned from a line to a curve. The new model allows slightly higher amounts of plasma glucose concentration for younger and older people before predicting diabetes. People in the age 40-50 are predicted with diabetes at slightly lower amounts of plasma glucose concentration.
```{r Part5, fig.width=12}
```
